appearance.explanation: Hnuaipui is the Mizo crop/harvest sacrifice - 'hnua' denotes the standing paddy crop, and other MPSC papers in the same corpus describe 'hnuaipui' as the sacrifice in which a full-grown pig is killed and as the offering made to the god of sun and rain. record.question: A pig reared specially for religious sacrifice is called
record.explanation: Vawkpui denotes the full-grown (reared) pig: the 1913 Lushai-English dictionary has 'Vok-pui, a sow', the English-Mizo dictionary glosses 'sow' as 'vawkpui, vawknu puitling' (a female pig reared for fattening) and contrasts it with a 'farrow', a pig 'that has not been reared', and the Mizo-Tawngupa dictionary entry 'Vawkpui phurh' describes this pig being kept apart and reared before it is killed and offered, the same full-grown female pig killed in the hnuaipui sacrifice. Confidence is low because the competing phrase 'vawkpa sut nghak' (killing/offering a pig to the deity) could also be read as a name for the sacrificial pig, and the OCR of the Mizo dictionary is partly corrupt.

record.explanation: Held. The printed page 9 confirms the stem and the four Mizo options, and 'Thingfar zan' is attested as a Mizo song in Mizo-language literature (the 1987 anthology 'Mizo Thawnthu' has the phrase 'An thingfar zan chuan nula' in a folktale), but I could not find any source stating which of the listed items it corresponds to; 'Dawino chhui' is a priestly rite and 'Chawngchen' a song/dance ('Chawngchen zai', 'Chawngchen lam'), and 'Lawithat zan' and 'Mitthi lumen zan' are songs, but no link to 'Thingfar zan' is documented. record.question: 'Tungchaw' literally means
record.explanation: The 1913 Lushai-English dictionary (Lorrain & Savidge) lists 'Tung-chaw, (n.) a Lushai bedpost' (and 'Tung-chaw-kua', a hole in a Lushai bedpost), so the term literally denotes the traditional Mizo bedpost - 'tung' being the bed post and 'chaw' the Lushai word for rice/food, the bed being a bamboo one.
